paragraphs: Random forests can predict well while giving misleading accounts of which inputs matter. A common importance measure, Mean Decrease Impurity (MDI), can assign substantial importance to noisy features. This paper studies that bias theoretically and develops a revised measure intended to improve feature selection.

The theoretical analysis gives a tight bound on the expected importance assigned to noisy features for a finite sample. It shows that deeper trees have greater expected feature selection bias than shallower trees. The authors then derive a different mathematical expression for MDI, which makes it possible to construct a correction using out-of-bag samples: observations excluded from the training sample for a particular tree.

The resulting measure, MDI-oob, achieves reported state-of-the-art feature selection performance on simulated data and a genomic ChIP dataset, for both deep and shallow trees. The contribution connects an explanation of why the original measure is biased with a practical correction, helping separate predictive model performance from the reliability of its feature rankings.
neurips-2019-a-debiased-mdi-feature-impo.tldr: MDI-oob uses out-of-bag samples to reduce random forests’ feature importance bias, supported by theory and feature selection experiments.

paragraphs: In continuous control, an agent chooses actions from a continuous range. The paper examines a restriction of policy gradient methods: they require access to the policy’s probability distribution, which constrains how that policy is represented. The authors show that optimization within such parametric distribution classes produces local movement through action space and can lead to suboptimal solutions.

Their alternative is a distributional framework capable of representing arbitrary distributions over continuous actions. They use it to build Generative Actor Critic, or GAC, a generative policy trained through an off-policy actor-critic approach. Its distinguishing feature is that learning does not require knowledge of the underlying action probability distribution.

This changes the representation available to the policy and addresses the restriction identified in the analysis. In continuous-domain experiments, GAC performs comparably to, and often better than, the state-of-the-art baselines considered. These findings support the practical value of the framework without establishing that every learned policy reaches a globally optimal solution.
neurips-2019-distributional-policy-optim.tldr: Generative Actor Critic learns flexible continuous-action policies without requiring their probability distributions and often outperforms the evaluated baselines.

paragraphs: A seller repeatedly running auctions must learn how item characteristics affect buyers’ values. Buyers can exploit this learning process by bidding strategically to influence future reserve prices. The paper studies how to learn prices despite that incentive, measuring lost revenue against a seller who already knows buyers’ differing preferences.

The proposed policies estimate preferences from auction outcomes instead of submitted bids. They also control how much each auction outcome can affect reserve prices over the longer term. These choices address the connection between current buyer behavior and future pricing, which makes ordinary learning from sales data vulnerable to manipulation.

Contextual Robust Pricing, or CORP, assumes the seller knows the market noise distribution and has regret bounded by O(d log(Td) log(T)). Stable CORP handles an unknown distribution within an ambiguity set, with regret O(√(d log(Td)) T^(2/3)). Here d counts contextual dimensions and T counts auction periods. Both bounds describe sublinear growth in cumulative regret for fixed d, under their respective settings.
neurips-2019-dynamic-incentive-aware-lea.tldr: CORP and SCORP learn reserve prices from auction outcomes while limiting strategic buyers’ influence on future prices.

paragraphs: Greedy clustering methods are attractive because they are fast, straightforward to implement, and supported by approximation guarantees. Their weakness is sensitivity to noisy points or outliers. This paper asks whether familiar methods can retain their useful guarantees while becoming robust to those points, without requiring a fundamentally different clustering procedure.

The authors modify greedy algorithms for both k-means and k-center clustering. For k-means++, they show that applying a simple threshold to distances is sufficient to obtain an O(log k) approximation to the objective. They also establish related results for k-center. The theoretical contribution is that robustness can coexist with guarantees nearly matching those of the established greedy approaches.

Experiments examine implementation practicality, scaling, and the ability to identify noise added to a dataset. The reported results support the algorithms’ ease of use and scalability. Together, the theory and experiments make the case for small, targeted modifications to widely used clustering procedures when outliers would otherwise distort their choices.
neurips-2019-greedy-sampling-for-approxi.tldr: Simple modifications make greedy k-means and k-center algorithms robust to outliers while retaining nearly the same approximation guarantees.

paragraphs: The paper studies multiple agents facing a shared bandit problem and exchanging messages through a communication network. The goal is to control each agent’s individual regret, so cooperation must benefit agents separately rather than merely producing a favorable aggregate result. The setting is nonstochastic, rather than assuming rewards follow a fixed random distribution.

The authors develop algorithms whose expected regret for each agent is bounded, up to logarithmic factors, by √((1 + K/|N(v)|)T). Here K is the number of actions, T is the number of time steps, and |N(v)| is the number of that agent’s neighbors. The bound explicitly connects an agent’s guarantee to its local communication opportunities.

They handle both globally known and unknown communication graphs. In the unknown case, agents need only their own neighbor sets and an upper bound on the total number of agents. The regret guarantees differ by just a logarithmic factor between these settings, showing that extensive knowledge of the network is not required for the stated individual guarantees.
neurips-2019-individual-regret-in-cooper.tldr: Cooperative bandit algorithms give each agent regret guarantees tied to its neighbors, even without full knowledge of the communication network.

paragraphs: A learned representation can devote multiple parts to overlapping information, leaving other useful information underrepresented. This paper proposes Information Competing Process, or ICP, to encourage richer representations. Its central idea is to make separate parts develop useful information under different constraints before combining them for the final task.

ICP divides a representation into two parts and applies different mutual information constraints to them. Each part must independently accomplish the downstream task in a competitive setting designed to prevent it from learning the same task information as the other. The parts are then brought together so their different contributions can support the task jointly.

The authors evaluate this approach on image classification and image reconstruction in supervised and self-supervised settings. The experiments demonstrate potential for learning representations that both distinguish relevant categories and separate underlying information. The findings support competition followed by combination as a useful strategy for representation diversity, rather than establishing a universal guarantee that the learned parts will be fully disentangled.
neurips-2019-information-competing-proce.tldr: ICP trains competing parts of a representation under different information constraints, then combines them to capture more diverse task-relevant information.

paragraphs: Quadrature approximates an integral using function values at selected points. This paper studies that problem for functions in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, or RKHS, where a kernel specifies the function space’s structure. The main question is how to choose evaluation points and relate the resulting integration error to that structure.

The authors sample points using a projection determinantal point process, or DPP. They construct its kernel from a truncated and saturated version of the RKHS kernel. This connection between the sampling mechanism and the function space lets them derive relatively tight error bounds that depend on the spectrum of the original kernel.

Experiments compare this approach with herding, Bayesian quadrature, and continuous leverage score sampling. The numerical results support the usefulness of DPP-based quadrature and suggest convergence faster than the theoretical bounds in some cases. That distinction matters: the bounds provide analytical guarantees, while the faster rates are observations from particular numerical settings.
neurips-2019-kernel-quadrature-with-dpps.tldr: Sampling quadrature points with a DPP tied to the function-space kernel yields spectral error bounds and promising numerical performance.

paragraphs: Image classifiers can make incorrect decisions after small changes to their inputs. This paper investigates whether visual representations measured in brains can guide convolutional neural networks toward more robust features. The approach uses neural data as a training constraint on how a classifier represents images internally.

The researchers presented natural images to mice and recorded responses from thousands of neurons in visual cortical areas. They trained predictive models on these responses to reduce the effect of variable neural activity. From the models’ predictions, they estimated representational similarity for millions of image pairs, then penalized intermediate CNN representations that departed from those neural similarity relationships.

The resulting classifiers preserved baseline performance on standard image benchmarks while performing substantially better on noisy images than baseline or control models. They also showed improved robustness to adversarial attacks. These findings indicate that the relationships among brain responses to different images can provide a useful inductive bias for robust classification, without requiring the classifier to reproduce every recorded neural response.
neurips-2019-learning-from-brains-how-to.tldr: Regularizing image classifiers with mouse visual-cortex similarity patterns improves robustness while preserving standard benchmark performance.

paragraphs: Tasks that provide a reward only at completion can demand many learning attempts because the agent receives little guidance along the way. Expert demonstrations can help, but supervised imitation may still leave errors that require further correction. This paper uses expert trajectories both to initialize behavior and to discover intermediate goals.

The method learns a function that partitions the state space into subgoals. Those subgoals support an externally specified reward function for reinforcement learning. Training first follows an imitation learning stage, then switches to reinforcement learning with the discovered subgoals to alleviate imitation errors. A second learned function modulates subgoal predictions for states that are poorly represented in the demonstrations.

The authors report solving complex goal-oriented tasks that other reinforcement learning, imitation learning, and combined approaches in the literature could not solve. The stated finding supports using demonstrations as a source of task structure as well as behavior examples. The additional modulation addresses the specific difficulty of making subgoal predictions beyond well-covered demonstration states.
neurips-2019-learning-from-trajectories-.tldr: The method discovers subgoals from expert trajectories and uses them to guide reinforcement learning after an initial imitation stage.

paragraphs: Distributed neural network training requires assigning computations to devices. Learning a good assignment separately for every computation graph can create substantial overhead. Placeto addresses this problem by learning a placement policy that can transfer to new graphs, making the learned decision process reusable.

The policy improves a placement iteratively instead of producing an entire assignment in one step. It also uses graph embeddings to represent relevant computation structure without depending on node labels for indexing. These design choices let the policy work with graph structure in a way intended to support efficient training and application to unseen graphs.

Experiments show that Placeto needs up to 6.1 times fewer training steps to find placements matching or improving upon the best placements found by prior approaches. The authors also demonstrate transfer without retraining to unseen graphs from the same family used to learn the policy. That family-specific result is the practical generalization claim: repeated placement problems within a family can avoid training a new policy from scratch.
neurips-2019-learning-generalizable-devi.tldr: Placeto learns iterative device-placement policies that transfer without retraining to unseen computation graphs from the same family.

paragraphs: Estimating human poses throughout a video typically demands expensive frame-by-frame annotations. PoseWarper learns from videos labeled only every k frames, using relationships between frames to extend the value of those sparse labels. Its goal is both to propagate pose annotations and to improve pose estimation over time.

During training, the network predicts the pose in a labeled frame using features from an unlabeled frame. Deformable convolutions let it learn the alignment between their poses implicitly. At inference, reversing the application direction transfers information from manually labeled frames to unlabeled ones, making dense annotations possible from a small set of manual labels.

The reported propagation comparison favors PoseWarper over optical-flow methods in both size and accuracy: 6 million versus 39 million parameters, and 88.7% versus 83.8% mAP. Training a pose estimator with the propagated labels further improves accuracy. The network can also aggregate information from neighboring frames at inference, yielding reported state-of-the-art results on PoseTrack2017 and PoseTrack2018.
neurips-2019-learning-temporal-pose-esti.tldr: PoseWarper learns temporal pose alignment from sparse video labels to propagate annotations and improve pose estimation.

paragraphs: Optimizing an objective in a stochastic environment can require estimating derivatives when the dynamics are unknown or too difficult to handle directly. This becomes more demanding when learning needs derivatives beyond the first order. Loaded DiCE develops an objective that works with automatic differentiation to produce low-variance, unbiased derivative estimates at any order.

The objective accommodates arbitrary advantage estimators, allowing control over bias and variance when function approximation is used. This separates the general derivative construction from choices about how learning signals are estimated. The paper also proposes discounting the influence of more distant causal dependencies, providing another way to trade bias against variance in higher-order derivatives.

The authors demonstrate correctness and usefulness in analytically tractable Markov decision processes and in meta-reinforcement learning for continuous control. The contribution is therefore both a derivative-estimation construction and a set of controls for practical estimation. The unbiased result should be distinguished from deliberately biased variants introduced to reduce variance.
neurips-2019-loaded-dice-trading-off-bia.tldr: Loaded DiCE supports automatic estimation of derivatives at any order and offers controls for trading bias against variance.

paragraphs: Short event sequences provide limited evidence for predicting what happens next. When relationships between sequences are also available, those connections can help determine which sequences should share information. HARMLESS uses a collection of short sequences together with a relational network to learn distinct but related event models.

The method combines a hierarchical Bayesian mixture model with Hawkes processes. Its representation of mixed communities in the relational network encourages knowledge sharing while allowing adaptation to each individual sequence. This matters because pooling information and preserving differences are both central to the problem: the sequences need not all follow the same event-generating behavior.

The authors also develop a stochastic variational meta-EM algorithm intended to make inference efficient enough for large problems. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show better future-event prediction than the existing methods considered. The findings support incorporating relationships directly into sequence modeling, so that scarce observations for one sequence can be interpreted alongside information from related sequences.
neurips-2019-meta-learning-with-relation.tldr: HARMLESS uses relational communities to share knowledge across short event sequences while adapting a predictive model to each sequence.

paragraphs: Invertible neural networks must support recovering an input from its transformed representation. MintNet proposes a construction based on simple building blocks and new composition rules, producing a broad range of invertible architectures, including designs resembling ResNets. The aim is to combine architectural flexibility with operations needed for both classification and generation.

The inverse is computed through a parallelizable iterative procedure that is locally convergent and reported to be fast in practice. The network’s Jacobian determinant can also be calculated analytically and efficiently. That determinant makes the architecture usable as a flow model, where transformations support evaluating the probability assigned to data.

For classification, the networks are competitive with ResNets on MNIST and CIFAR-10. As generative models, they achieve reported competitive likelihoods of 0.98, 3.32, and 4.06 bits per dimension on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet 32×32, respectively. These results demonstrate flexibility across the two uses, while the inversion guarantee remains specifically local rather than a claim of convergence from every starting point.
neurips-2019-mintnet-building-invertible.tldr: MintNet constructs flexible invertible networks with efficient Jacobian determinants and a fast, locally convergent inversion procedure.

paragraphs: Protecting data during computation and protecting individuals when results are released are related but distinct requirements. This paper combines trusted execution environments, which protect data contents during computation, with differentially private queries, which provide record privacy in released outputs. It focuses on queries that use samples of a dataset.

Sampling is attractive because using only a subset can strengthen privacy guarantees through privacy amplification. However, obtaining that benefit inside a trusted execution environment requires keeping the selected records’ indices secret. The authors design efficient secure versions of common sampling algorithms to address this requirement, making the sampling process part of the privacy design.

Experiments compare differentially private models trained using shuffling and sampling on MNIST and CIFAR-10. The reported accuracy is the same, while sampling provides stronger privacy guarantees. The result supports secure sampling as a way to improve privacy in the evaluated setting without sacrificing the observed predictive accuracy.
neurips-2019-oblivious-sampling-algorith.tldr: Secure sampling algorithms preserve secret sample indices, enabling stronger privacy guarantees with unchanged reported accuracy in the evaluated models.

paragraphs: Explanations of model predictions and adversarial examples are often studied as separate ways to understand model behavior. Earlier work had explored their relationship mainly through experiments. This paper establishes a theoretical connection, giving a mathematical account of how the two kinds of information relate.

The connection uses a generalized form of hitting set duality. A hitting set intersects every set in a specified collection; duality connects complementary collections through that relationship. The paper extends a form of this reasoning previously observed in model-based diagnosis and knowledge compilation to explanations and adversarial examples.

The authors also propose algorithms that compute adversarial examples from explanations and explanations from adversarial examples. This makes the relationship constructive: it provides a route for deriving one kind of object from the other, beyond observing that they are correlated in experiments. The contribution supplies a shared theoretical basis for the two problems and corresponding procedures for moving between them.
neurips-2019-on-relating-explanations-an.tldr: A generalized hitting set duality connects explanations and adversarial examples and supports algorithms for computing either from the other.

paragraphs: A graph neural network’s expressive power can be studied by asking which graphs it distinguishes or which graph functions it approximates. The paper connects these perspectives and proves their equivalence. This links structural discrimination with approximation of functions that remain unchanged when graph nodes are relabeled.

The authors develop a common framework using sigma-algebras to describe representation power. It accommodates both viewpoints and supports comparisons among classes of graph neural networks and other graph methods. The value of this framework is that architectural limitations can be examined through a shared mathematical description rather than separate kinds of tests.

One concrete result shows that order-2 Graph G-invariant networks cannot distinguish non-isomorphic regular graphs with the same degree. The proposed extension, Ring-GNN, succeeds in distinguishing these graphs and is also demonstrated on tasks involving real-world datasets. The architecture therefore addresses a particular proven expressive limitation; the abstract does not claim it distinguishes every possible pair of non-isomorphic graphs.
neurips-2019-on-the-equivalence-between-.tldr: The paper unifies graph discrimination and function approximation, then introduces Ring-GNN to overcome a specific expressive limitation.

paragraphs: Best-arm identification asks how many observations are needed to select the best option at a specified confidence level. This paper studies a Markovian version, where observations have temporal dependence, within a one-parameter family of bandit models. Its goal is to characterize sampling complexity in that structured setting.

The authors derive lower bounds tailored to individual problem instances, both for finite samples and asymptotically. These extend corresponding bounds from independent, identically distributed observations. They also analyze Track-and-Stop, a strategy originally developed for that independent setting, and prove that its asymptotic sampling complexity is within a factor of four of the lower bound.

The analysis builds on exponential families of stochastic matrices and establishes properties of those families. It additionally produces a new optimal concentration inequality for Markov chains. The results connect an unavoidable sampling requirement with an achievable strategy, while the factor-four statement makes clear that the analyzed strategy is not shown to match the lower bound exactly.
neurips-2019-optimal-best-markovian-arm-.tldr: For one-parameter Markovian bandits, the paper derives sampling lower bounds and places Track-and-Stop within a factor of four asymptotically.

paragraphs: The paper studies a connection between learning with differential privacy and learning online. Previous results established that private learnability implies online learnability, but that implication left a computational question unresolved. Even if an online learner exists, can it be obtained efficiently from an efficient private learner?

The authors answer this question in the setting of pure differential privacy. They give an efficient black-box reduction from differentially private learning to online learning from expert advice. A black-box reduction uses the private learner as an available component, making the result a conversion between learning capabilities rather than a separate construction for each learner’s internal design.

The significance is the preservation of computational efficiency across that conversion. The result strengthens an existence relationship into an algorithmic one: an efficient private learner can support an efficient online learner in the stated setting. Its scope is specifically pure differential privacy, which is the privacy regime in which the paper resolves the question.
neurips-2019-private-learning-implies-on.tldr: An efficient black-box reduction shows that efficient learning under pure differential privacy implies efficient online learning from expert advice.

paragraphs: A neural network’s prediction can be uncertain because the target itself varies or because the input falls outside familiar data. This paper offers single-model estimates for these two forms, called aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. The approach avoids needing an ensemble of deep models or retraining those models.

For aleatoric uncertainty, Simultaneous Quantile Regression learns all conditional quantiles of a target variable through a proposed loss function. Quantiles describe different positions in the target’s conditional distribution and can be used to form well-calibrated prediction intervals. This provides information about the range of plausible outcomes rather than just a single predicted value.

For epistemic uncertainty, Orthonormal Certificates are diverse, nonconstant functions that return zero on all training samples. They return nonzero values on out-of-distribution examples, providing an uncertainty signal. The authors report state-of-the-art performance and emphasize computational attractiveness. The two components address different uncertainty sources within the paper’s single-model approach.
neurips-2019-single-model-uncertainties-.tldr: Quantile regression and orthonormal certificates estimate two forms of uncertainty without ensembling or retraining deep models.

paragraphs: SPoC translates pseudocode into executable programs under the assumption that each pseudocode line corresponds to one code line. Instead of accepting only the highest-ranked translation, it searches over candidate combinations and uses compilation and supplied test cases to check whether a candidate succeeds.

Compilation errors account for 88.7% of failures during the paper’s best-first search. To make search more targeted, the authors learn to predict which program line caused a failure. The search can then concentrate on alternative translations for that line, using failure information to decide where another attempt is most useful.

The evaluation introduces a dataset of 18,356 C++ programs paired with human-written pseudocode and tests. With a budget of 100 compilations, search raises synthesis success from 25.6% for the top translation to 44.7%. This shows the value of testing alternatives and using compiler feedback under the stated line-alignment assumption. Success here means producing code that compiles and passes the provided tests.
neurips-2019-spoc-search-based-pseudocod.tldr: SPoC uses compilation feedback to guide pseudocode-to-code search, raising test-passing synthesis success within a fixed compilation budget.

paragraphs: Risk scores can influence decisions through rankings as well as binary classifications. Fairness checks focused on a classification threshold or performance within each group may therefore overlook differences in how people from different groups are ordered. This paper studies that issue through ranking positive examples above negative examples.

The proposed xAUC disparity compares two probabilities: a positive example from one protected group ranking above a negative example from another, and the corresponding comparison with the groups exchanged. Their difference captures asymmetry in cross-group ranking. The authors also decompose ranking loss into terms involving this discrepancy and terms reflecting predictive ability within each group.

Audits of recidivism, income, and cardiac arrest prediction reveal disparities that are not apparent from within-group predictive performance alone. The finding shows why comparing each group’s internal accuracy can leave part of a score’s behavior unexamined. xAUC supplies a specific additional view of fairness for applications where comparisons across groups affect how scores are used.
neurips-2019-the-fairness-of-risk-scores.tldr: xAUC measures cross-group ranking disparities that can remain hidden when risk scores are evaluated only within each group.

paragraphs: This paper examines what graph convolutional networks can learn about graph structure through graph moments, which encode paths of different lengths. It finds that these networks can be restrictive in their ability to learn such properties. Multiple layers and nonlinear activations alone do not prevent failures when the architecture is poorly designed.

The authors analyze expressiveness theoretically and develop a modular architecture combining different propagation rules. Propagation determines how information travels through the graph, so changing these rules changes the structural information available to the model. The proposed design can distinguish graphs from different graph-generation models even when the graphs are small, a difficult setting highlighted by the paper.

The investigation suggests that depth matters more than width for this task, with deeper networks better able to learn higher-order graph moments. It also identifies combining modules with different propagation rules as critical to representation power. The findings provide architectural guidance tied to learning graph topology, rather than asserting that increasing depth alone solves every expressive limitation.
neurips-2019-understanding-the-represent.tldr: Analysis through graph moments motivates modular graph networks and highlights the importance of depth and varied propagation rules.

paragraphs: Reducing high-dimensional time series to a few coordinates can reveal meaningful dynamics, but methods that ignore time may instead emphasize noise. Dynamical Components Analysis, or DCA, makes temporal predictability central to selecting those coordinates. It combines linear dimensionality reduction with the idea that useful features help predict their surrounding context.

DCA seeks a linear subspace that maximizes predictive information, defined as the mutual information between the past and future. In plain terms, it favors a compact representation whose earlier values retain information about what comes next. The method therefore evaluates the representation through temporal relationships rather than disregarding the order of observations.

On synthetic examples, DCA extracts dynamical structure better than commonly used linear methods. Across several real datasets, its dimensions are more useful for predicting future states and decoding auxiliary variables. The reported results support extracting dynamics from noisy data while keeping the computational efficiency and geometric interpretability associated with linear dimensionality reduction.
neurips-2019-unsupervised-discovery-of-t.tldr: DCA finds linear representations that maximize information shared between past and future, improving extraction of dynamics from noisy time series.

paragraphs: An intelligent agent benefits from representations that capture the underlying state of its environment rather than only the appearance of an observation. This paper investigates learning those representations without reward supervision. It contributes both a learning method and a benchmark for checking how much true state information a representation preserves.

The method maximizes mutual information between features from a neural observation encoder at different spatial locations and times. This encourages information to be shared across features that describe distinct parts or moments of the observations. The training signal comes from those relationships, allowing representation learning without a task reward specifying which features matter.

The benchmark uses Atari 2600 games and evaluates representations by how well they capture ground-truth state. The authors compare their method with generative and contrastive representation learning approaches. The abstract does not state a winning method; its reported contribution is an approach and evaluation framework centered on recovering environment state, with the authors arguing that this framework can support future research.
neurips-2019-unsupervised-state-represen.tldr: The paper learns reward-free Atari representations through spatial and temporal mutual information and evaluates how well they capture true environment state.
